title: Preface
summary: OCR-garbled CIA Studies in Intelligence article (Winter 1977, Vol. 21 No. 4) by Dr. Kenneth A. Kress reviewing CIA involvement in parapsychology as an intelligence collection possibility. Covers the Agency's sponsored research, biases and ridicule that hindered it, political sensitivity of unusual research contracts, the polarized reactions (belief versus rejection), unexplained but incomplete data showing occasional results, focus on psychokinesis and remote viewing, and historical military/intelligence interest in ESP including a 1952 Pentagon lecture and 1961 reports. Includes standard CIA disclaimer that views are the authors' own.

title: PARAPSYCHOLOGY IN INTELLIGENCE: A PERSONAL REVIEW AND CONCLUSIONS
summary: A declassified CIA-era paper by Dr. Kenneth A. Kress reviews the Agency's history of sponsoring parapsychology research (ESP and psychokinesis, including remote viewing) for intelligence collection. It covers the 1952 Pentagon ESP lecture, early CIA interest, the 1972-1975 SRI-run projects with subjects like Pat Price, a dispute over a four-state ESP teaching machine, and the Semipalatinsk test-site remote viewing experiment. The author concludes results were tantalizing but inconclusive, the projects faced skepticism, fraud concerns, and sensitivity, and the work was eventually tabled amid Watergate-era scrutiny.

title: amphi
summary: A declassified CIA document reviews the agency's parapsychology (remote viewing) program. It covers an early skeptical critique, a physicist's favorable reassessment, and operational tests, including Pat Price locating Libyan and embassy sites. It records the program's termination, the Libyan requirement follow-up, and Price's death. It also covers later interest from DIA, the Army, DARPA, the Navy, and the Air Force, plus public disclosure. The author concludes the phenomenon remains unexplained and controversial, and urges agencies to fund long-term basic research rather than applications-driven testing.
